pr_title: drivers: watchdog: TI CC13xx/CC26xx watchdog timer support
pr_body:
Implemented new WDT driver for TI CC13xx/CC26xx family using HAL TI routines.
Supports interrupts & MCU soft reset on timeout.

Follow up from stale / closed PR #39332 :(
Fixes https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/39331

Tested on my CC1352P1 LaunchXL using samples/drivers/watchdog.
pr_comments:
Hi @niflostancu

> rewritten init code to use `DT_INST_FOREACH_STATUS_OKAY`;

I see that this was suggested here by @cfriedt and you did it also in your another PR #49229 but I really don't understand this approach. From what I understand, this in result allows to generate several instances of the same driver for separated blocks of the same hardware, based on the DTS. But... you are still using the TI's driverlib (at least for the wdt that's only incline functions accessing some registers, not sure about the ADC if there is anything already in the ROM) which doesn't even allow to pass register base to functions. Plus, in case of this series of SOCs, there is just one watchdog and I doubt there will be anything new with more than one. So in this case, we have some extra code, e.g. the `reg` which is not used at all.
@cfriedt could you please explain motivation behind this suggestion to use `DT_INST_FOREACH_STATUS_OKAY` instead of `DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE`?

> * implemented NMI mode (using a new boolean DTSI property: `interrupt-nmi`; hope that's the best way to do it);

I was planning to handle it as a Kconfig option. No opinion on the DTS property but I'm pretty sure that introducing something like this would need to be first discussed with a wider audience and defined somewhere in bindings for the `watchdog` subsystem.

> Note: as various TI forum posts suggest [1] (I couldn't find any explicit mentions in the Reference), the watchdog clock is always paused during sleep, so there is nothing to be done in this case (I avoided any option checks for this to be permissive).

I found it in datasheet (not the reference manual):

> The watchdog timer is used to regain control if the system operates incorrectly due to software errors. It is typically used to generate an interrupt to and reset of the device for the case where periodic monitoring of the system components and tasks fails to verify proper functionality. The watchdog timer runs on a 1.5 MHz clock rate and cannot be stopped once enabled. **The watchdog timer pauses to run in Standby power mode and when a debugger halts the device**.

Watchdog is also listed under `Power Management` in `Power Modes` table in this document. That's why I have some doubts and still plan to do more tests.
Source: https://www.ti.com/lit/gpn/cc1352r

I have also some additional comments, will add them in code.

Cheers,
Piotr

Alternatively, `DEVICE_DT_GET_ANY` or `DEVICE_DT_GET_ONE`.

<_also insert your favorite "rules are to be broken" quote ;)_ >

Regarding my contributions, I assure you they are thoroughly tested on real hardware (I already use them in production for over a year) and I am 100% available for fixing any bugs discovered.

issue_context.title: ti: cc13xx_cc26xx: watchdog timer driver
issue_context.body:
**Is your enhancement proposal related to a problem? Please describe.**
A watchdog driver for TI CC13xx / CC26xx MCUs would be nice :D  

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Implementation in upcoming PR...

review_comments:
I have some doubts here, see: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/include/zephyr/drivers/watchdog.h#L161

We allow to `disable` this watchdog (but only by disabling generating the reset) so the `setup` can be called again. But is this a correct approach? In fact, this type of watchdog cannot be stopped.

Yeah, the primary use case for this was to be able change the timeout dynamically.
A Zephyr Watchdog API behavior change like being able to call `install_timeout` after setup would be a better way, though...

Or, we could further _emulate_ the watchdog being stopped by defining a boolean flag that gets set when `wdt_disable` is called then preventing the execution of the user callback (note: the interrupt handler will still fire).
